reason: The court held that a collateral defence to the grant failed because invalidity was not proved, but the quote is an external administrative-law passage and does not support the burden point.
The court construed section 4(1) of the Trusts Ordinance in deciding that the pleaded constructive trust was not unlawful merely because tax avoidance was alleged.
The Rent Act holding is accurately stated, but the judgment construed section 2(4)(c), not the tagged SRC028-s4 provision.
The court adopted the ambiguity principle when identifying the partition corpus, but the supporting quote is a quotation from Appuhamy v Gallella rather than this court's own holding.
The judgment addresses non-objection to documents, but the quote is only a citation list about cursus curiae and the statement omits the read-in or admission-stage conditions.
On the facts, the court held that the appellant had proved a 3-foot right of way by necessity and prescriptive user for over ten years.
The court construed section 4 to include disturbance as dispossession in appropriate circumstances, but the statement drops that limiting qualification.
The quoted observation is correct, but the holding was that other evidence could prove an LDO permit and the judgment concerned section 19(2), not SRC050-s2.
The section 4 pre-emption rule was applied, but the statement omits the material Thesawalamai context and related statutory limits.
The rei vindicatio burden was part of the court's reasoning, but the quote is a citation to an earlier case and the tagged CPC issue-framing section is not the source of the rule.

The court applied the new-ground-on-appeal rule under CPC section 150, but the quote is from another case and the statement omits the requirement that all needed material be before the appellate court.
The court held that a co-owner could eject the trespasser without joining other co-owners, but CPC section 147 was only procedural and not the provision construed for that rule.
The attornment rule was the court's holding, but the judgment did not construe Rent Act section 7 for that proposition.
The statement and quote match the court's holding, but the operative provision was Trusts Ordinance section 112, not SRC059-s102.
The court applied the rei vindicatio title burden, but the supporting sentence is quoted from Wanigaratne v Juwanis Appuhamy.
The refund rule was applied after tsunami frustration, but the selected quote is only the disposition and omits the direct-and-immediate causation limitation.
The section 44 proposition is correctly quoted, but the appeal was decided because the possessory action was within time and limitation had not been pleaded.
The court found no constructive trust on the total facts, while the statement turns one evidential factor into an overbroad rule and the quote is merely factual.
The court adopted the synonym conclusion for this temple dispute, but the selected quote reports the conclusion of an earlier judgment rather than this court's own holding.
The court applied section 33 of the Partition Law and held that improvements should be allotted to the improving co-owner only so far as practicable.
The court used the deed-description principle to decide that the appellant's undivided corpus was sufficiently identified.
Section 8 of the Land Settlement Ordinance was decisive, but the statement omits the statutory proviso for fraud or wilful suppression and the section 5(6) qualification.
The section 3 prescription rule was applied to non-co-owner defendants, but the statement omits adverse or independent possession and absence of acknowledgment.
The court applied section 402 to non-prosecution, but the selected quote is from Supramanium v Symons rather than this court's own holding.
The commissioner's plan supported the factual finding of encroachment, but that is evidential fact-finding rather than a ratio rule of law.
